title: Tourism Marketing
summary: Marketing is the sum of all activities that direct the flow of goods and services from producer to consumer (American Marketing Association); the British Institute of Marketing calls it 'the management process responsible for identifying, anticipating and satisfying customer requirements profitably'. In its simplest form it is a process of achieving voluntary exchanges between customers and producers. Tourism marketing is the process of achieving voluntary exchanges between tourists and organisations; it begins with understanding tourists' needs and includes designing, promoting and selling a tour package. It uses the basic principles of marketing and is not a separate discipline.

Marketing vs selling: marketing is a market-oriented approach that starts with the buyer and focuses on the buyer's needs; it satisfies customers, is the broader term and price is decided by the consumer. Selling is a product-oriented approach that starts with the seller, focuses on converting the product into cash, is a part of marketing and cost determines price.

Features of tourism products (services): inseparability (produced and consumed together), perishability (an empty seat or room cannot be stored), ownership (no transfer of ownership; the customer buys an experience) and heterogeneity (variation because of the human element).

Functions: market research (systematic investigation of facts for marketing; finds who tourists are, their tastes and when they will buy), product planning and development (tourism product is composite), segmentation (identifying groups of buyers with different needs, e.g. religious tourists), promotion (advertising, publicity, personal selling and sales promotion) and selling (direct, retail, agency, tele-sales, door-to-door, business-to-business, mail order and online). The marketing mix is the set of controllable tools: the four Ps (product, price, promotion, place); for services three more: people, physical evidence and process.

Macro environment (external, beyond the firm's control): political (laws, regulations; e.g. FDI in retail), economic (purchasing power, inflation), demographic (population size, age, income, education), technological (internet booking) and socio-cultural (values, beliefs, customs). Micro environment (directly affects the firm's ability to serve customers): suppliers, consumers (the core of marketing), competitors (business rivals offering similar products) and intermediaries (wholesalers, retailers, agents).

Price is the amount of money customers pay to obtain a product; it is the only part of the mix that generates revenue. Penetration pricing: a low price to increase sales and market share, raised later (discourages competitors). Skimming: a high initial price lowered slowly for innovative products. Psychological pricing: e.g. Rs 999 instead of Rs 1,000. Promotional pricing: temporary low price below cost (e.g. a Delhi–Mumbai return for Rs 2,000 if travelled within a week). Discount pricing: price cuts in a season or for a quantity (winter clearance sale, 5% on Rs 1,000, buy two get one free).

Advertising is a non-personal, one-way, paid form of communication by an identified sponsor (Kotler); its purpose is awareness, interest, sales and attitude change; AIDAS stands for Attract attention, Interest, Desire, Action, Satisfaction. Features: paid form, impersonality (monologue), identified sponsor. Media: press (newspapers, magazines, brochures, leaflets), broadcast (radio, television, cinema, video), the internet (the latest), aerial advertising, and railway and off-the-wall media. Media criteria: reach, frequency, continuity, scheduling, immediacy, prestige, cost and audience.

Sales promotion covers incentives other than advertising, personal selling and publicity (cash discounts, free samples, exhibitions, contests, gifts, coupons); it is personal, aims at increasing sales, has limited scope and gives immediate feedback; advertising is impersonal, aims at creating demand, reaches a huge population and gives no immediate feedback. Objectives: increase sales of slow-moving and new products, attract and retain customers, launch products quickly, educate customers, motivate dealers and the sales force and improve dealer relations. Tourism examples: airline discounts, flyer clubs, hotel premiums and incentives to travel agents; joint promotions by airlines, hotels and car rentals.

A distribution channel makes the product available to the consumer; in tourism it is a system of linkages between tourists and suppliers: travel agents (retailers who buy from wholesalers and sell to tourists for a commission), national, state and local tourism agencies (provide maps, guides and bookings), tour operators and wholesalers (consolidators who buy in volume and make packages) and online travel companies or cybermediaries (makemytrip, yatra, cleartrip, ibibo). Customer Relationship Management (CRM) manages a company's interactions with current and future customers to build loyalty: collect information, build a customer database, obtain and analyse requirements, develop products accordingly and keep personal communication. Hotels use guest databases and profiles to personalise service.

vsa: Describe any two characteristics of tourism marketing.
Tourism marketing sells an experience, not a tangible product, so services are inseparable and perishable. There is no transfer of ownership and the service varies because humans are involved.
October 2025
Give two differences between marketing and selling.

Marketing is market-oriented and starts with the buyer's needs; selling is product-oriented and starts with the seller. Marketing is broader and includes selling; in marketing the consumer determines price.
What is meant by segmentation? Give an example.
Segmentation is identifying groups of buyers with different needs. For example a tour package designed for religious tourists serves one segment.
What is the marketing mix?
It is the set of controllable tools a firm blends to get the response it wants: product, price, promotion and place, with people, physical evidence and process added for services.
State any two features of advertising.
It is a paid form of communication. It is impersonal (one-way) and has an identified sponsor.
Name any two types of selling techniques.
Direct selling and retail selling (also agency, tele-sales, door-to-door, business-to-business, mail order and online).
What is promotional pricing? Give an example.
A temporary price below cost to increase short-term sales. Example: a Delhi–Mumbai return flight for Rs 2,000 if travelled within a week.
Who are the intermediaries in the marketing environment?
They are wholesalers, retailers and agents who help bring the product to the consumer and create place and time utility.
Explain what CRM is.
Customer Relationship Management is managing a company's interactions with current and future customers to build, maintain and sustain relations and loyalty.
sa: Explain the macro environment of tourism marketing (three factors).

(i) Political environment: laws and policies such as FDI affect business. (ii) Economic and demographic environment: purchasing power, inflation, population size and income. (iii) Technological and socio-cultural environment: internet booking and the values, beliefs and customs of society.
Distinguish between advertising and sales promotion (three points).

(i) Advertising is impersonal; sales promotion is personal. (ii) Advertising aims at creating demand; sales promotion aims at increasing sales. (iii) Advertising reaches a huge audience but gives no immediate feedback; sales promotion has limited scope and gives immediate feedback.
Explain any three methods of sales promotion in tourism.

(i) Discount coupons let consumers avail discounts on purchase. (ii) Free samples and trade shows or exhibitions create awareness. (iii) Price discounts by airlines, flyer clubs, hotel premiums and incentives to travel agents.

(i) Penetration pricing: a low price to gain market share. (ii) Skimming: a high price lowered slowly for innovative products. (iii) Psychological pricing (Rs 999) and discount pricing (seasonal sale).
Explain any three distribution channels in tourism.

(i) Travel agents are retailers who sell to tourists for a commission. (ii) Tour operators and wholesalers buy in volume and make packages. (iii) Online travel companies such as makemytrip and national, state and local tourism agencies.
la: Explain the functions of marketing with reference to tourism, in six points.

(i) Market research: systematic investigation to know tourists' needs. (ii) Product planning and development: designing and improving products such as tour packages. (iii) Segmentation: grouping tourists by needs, e.g. religious tourists. (iv) Promotion: informing and persuading through advertising, publicity, personal selling and sales promotion. (v) Selling: direct, retail, agency, tele-sales and online. (vi) The marketing mix of the four Ps plus people, physical evidence and process guides these functions.
Explain advertising and the media used in the tourism business, in six points.

(i) Advertising is a paid, impersonal, one-way communication by an identified sponsor. (ii) Its purpose is awareness, interest, sales and attitude change (AIDAS). (iii) Press media include newspapers, magazines, brochures and leaflets. (iv) Broadcast media include radio, television, cinema and video. (v) The internet is the latest and most effective medium. (vi) Aerial, railway and off-the-wall media are also used and media are chosen by reach, frequency and cost.
Explain Customer Relationship Management and its steps, in six points.

(i) CRM manages interactions with current and future customers. (ii) It aims at customer satisfaction and loyalty. (iii) It collects information and builds a customer database. (iv) It obtains and analyses customer requirements. (v) It develops products as per the requirements and keeps personal communication. (vi) Hotels use guest profiles to personalise service.
